extracted.intended_audience: Members of Congress, DOD procurement and personnel officials, policymakers, and auditors
extracted.subtask_description: Audit/review criteria used to evaluate Department of Defense functions converted to contractor performance under OMB Circular A-76, focusing on contract cost increases and effects on federal employees. Covers cost-comparison rules, causes of contract cost growth, required treatment of employee placement and transition costs, and sampling/evaluation methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: OMB Circular A-76 cost-comparison requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: With some exceptions, the circular requires a comparison of the cost of in-house versus contractor performance to determine who will do the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cost comparisons are the basic test under A-76 for whether to contract out. The report notes cost comparisons normally cover a 3-year period and that conversions should be justified by projected savings from those comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projected savings: determination and realization
rubrics_metrics.description: The cost comparisons for each function projected savings by contracting; subsequent contract costs (including modifications) should be compared to the contractors' bids used in the original cost comparison to determine whether projected savings were actually realized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach used: compare contract costs, plus or minus contract modifications, with the original contractors' bids used in the cost comparisons. If increases were caused by factors unique to contracting out (or would not have had a similar effect in-house), examine whether the increase exceeded the original estimated savings to conclude if savings were realized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include contract modifications and subsequent contract awards in cost evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Contract costs, including modifications and costs under subsequent contracts (e.g., recompetes or extensions), must be considered when assessing whether contracting produced the projected savings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The audit compared total contract costs over the A-76 comparison period (including contract extensions, settlements, and subsequent higher bids) to the original bid/estimated contract costs. When a function was combined under a later contract that did not allocate modification costs to specific functions, attribution problems can arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution of cost increases to additional work and workload growth
rubrics_metrics.description: Cost increases often resulted primarily from additional work (e.g., installation growth or added workload not in the original comparison) which required contractors to perform more than originally estimated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When additional work occurred after award, analysts must consider whether similar additional work and associated costs would have occurred had the function remained in-house; some increases are not unique to contracting and therefore do not necessarily invalidate projected savings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service Contract Act / prevailing wage impact
rubrics_metrics.description: The Service Contract Act of 1965 requires federal contractors to pay employees not less than the prevailing minimum wage as determined by the Department of Labor; contractor bids and in-house cost estimates do not include costs for future wage increases, so when prevailing wages increase, contracts are modified to reimburse contractors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating cost increases, analysts should recognize that wage increases affect both contractor and in-house costs; projected savings are not necessarily invalidated because comparable pay increases would have occurred in-house.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract errors or ambiguities (inadequate statement of work)
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors or ambiguities in contracts—often stemming from inadequate statements of work used to develop bids—can cause contract cost increases by requiring contract modifications to correct scope or quantities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: understating number of vehicles serviced led to modifications and increased costs. Where errors/ambiguities caused increases, such costs would not have occurred had the work remained in-house, and they reduce projected savings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recompetition and contractor performance as a cost driver
rubrics_metrics.description: Recompetition of contracts (often because initial contractors failed to perform satisfactorily or because of scope changes) can result in cost increases when new contractors' bids are higher or transition costs occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The audit found contracts recompeted on several functions; although recompetes raised costs in each case reviewed, some savings were still realized. Recompetition costs and performance failures should be tracked and considered in the overall evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish increases unique to contracting versus those that would occur in-house
rubrics_metrics.description: When contract costs rise, determine whether the increase was caused by a factor unique to contracting out or would have had a similar effect on in-house performance; only increases unique to contracting should be treated as contracting-related cost penalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The GAO examined reasons for increases and only counted as negating savings those increases that were unique to contracting (e.g., contractor claims due to contract errors). Where wage increases or added workload would have raised in-house costs similarly, they were not treated as contracting penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for hidden costs to displaced employees
rubrics_metrics.description: Hidden costs—costs not considered in cost comparisons, such as unemployment or welfare payments to displaced employees—should be identified and assessed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The GAO attempted to obtain this information but found it not readily available and sent questionnaires to involuntarily separated employees and those who went to work for contractors. Hidden social costs should be measured and reported separately if practical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency workforce placement obligations under A-76
rubrics_metrics.description: A-76 requires agencies to exert maximum effort to find available positions for displaced employees; give priority consideration for available positions within the agency; pay training and relocation costs when they will contribute to placement; and coordinate with other agencies to assist employees in finding positions. Agencies also must assure contractors give priority consideration to displaced employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation of contracting effects on employees should measure whether these obligations were followed and quantify placement outcomes (placements at same installation, other installation, retirement, contractor employment, involuntary separation, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of severance pay, relocation, retraining, and retention-of-grade/pay costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Costs the government incurs for severance pay, relocation, retraining, and retention of grade or pay when converting a function to contract should be considered in cost comparisons under A-76.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Severance eligibility: continuous service of at least 12 months and involuntary separation; amount based on basic pay, age, and years of service. Retention of grade/pay: employees placed in lower graded positions retain prior grade for 2 years and prior pay indefinitely; the government cost is the difference between the employee's pay and the amount normally paid to fill the position. These transition costs can be difficult to quantify but should be estimated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee outcome metrics (placement and separation statistics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure and report outcomes for affected employees: numbers/percentages obtaining other government positions, retiring (regular/early), resigning, employed by contractor, involuntarily separated, placed in non-federal positions, discharged, or deceased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report demographic breakdowns (gender, race/national origin, veteran status) for affected groups and subgroups (placed, contractor-employed, involuntarily separated). The GAO presented counts and percentages and used these to compare with DOD reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical projection and confidence for employee percentages
rubrics_metrics.description: Percentages calculated from the sample of affected employees can be projected to the universe of functions converted in the same fiscal year with stated confidence and error bounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GAO: percentages can be projected with a 95% confidence level and an error rate of plus or minus 12 percent; however, raw counts may not be projectable because of discrepancies in listings vs actual employees found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling and selection rationale for evaluating conversions
rubrics_metrics.description: When reviewing cost increases use a judgmental sample of functions contracted out for at least the A-76 comparison period (3 years) to allow comparison of contract costs and modifications; when reviewing employee effects use random sampling of recent conversions with attention to covering a large share of affected positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GAO used a judgmental sample of 20 functions for cost increases (chosen for variety of function types, sizes, services, and geography) and a random sample of 31 functions for employee effects (selected from fiscal year 1983 conversions after eliminating very small conversions and oversampling largest conversions to cover a high share of positions). Explain limitations and projection boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption that wage increases and additional work would raise in-house costs similarly
rubrics_metrics.description: For comparison purposes, assume costs for additional work and wage increases would be approximately equal whether performed in-house or by contracting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GAO applied this assumption in its calculations and reasoning: because government employees would have received pay increases and workload growth would have increased in-house costs, certain post-award increases do not necessarily negate projected savings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly document reasons for cost increases and quantify their impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and list causes of observed contract cost increases (contractor claims, work backlog, contract extensions at higher price, higher subsequent bids, parts/materials/operations costs, loss of production events, etc.) and quantify each category's contribution to total increase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GAO provides line-item breakdowns for many reviewed functions (e.g., Fort Dix: contractor claim, reimbursement for backlog, additional work, parts), illustrating the need for granular attribution to determine whether increases were contracting-specific or general.
